https://www.dw.com/en/denmark-data-of-mi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5No7n The hacker has not yet been apprehended [FILE: March 12, 2024] Image: Loïc Déquier/PHOTOPQR/SUD OUEST/picture alliance Advertisement Denmark 's national registry was hacked in an incident the authorities described as "extremely serious." Hackers secured access to personal information on millions of people, the country's digital affairs ministry said on Monday. The compromised information included names, addresses and social security numbers, known in Denmark as national registry numbers. The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised. This figure exceeds Denmark's population size because it includes people who have already died or emigrated, the Danish authorities said in a statement. The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The hackers have not yet been identified. The means they used to gain access has since been cut off. The ministry said it was first alerted to an "anomaly" in the system "during September." Information of deceased, emigrated people included Denmark has a population of roughly six million people. However, its national registry includes information of eleven million people, which includes the data of those deceased or people who have moved abroad and don't live in Denmark anymore. Christina Egelund, Denmark's digital affairs minister, said the incident's full extent will investigated by the authorities. "This is an extremely serious incident," Egelund said. "We are in the process of tracking the exact extent of this incident with all those affected." Minister Christina Egelund called the breach 'very serious' [FILE: May 3, 2024] Image: Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/IMAGO Danish news agency Ritzau reported that the register includes information on church membership, details of legal incapacitation and restrictions on legal capacity. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Ukraine Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin Frontline near Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine quiet for first time in years ahead of planned evacuation Europe live – latest updates Luke Harding and Pjotr Sauer Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.03 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A local ceasefire in a southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation appeared to be holding on Tuesday, with both sides ceasing drone attacks ahead of an apparent evacuation of about 2,000 trapped and desperate civilians. The temporary truce began at 3am in Russian-controlled Oleshky. The city sits on the Dnipro River and is about 3 miles from Kherson, a larger city on the opposite bank. Ukrainian troops recaptured Kherson in autumn 2022 . Witnesses reported that the deadly frontline across the river was quiet for the first time in four years. The pause in fighting is due to last until 11pm on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said, and represents a significant if limited moment of de-escalation. Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, held what they described as a “frank and substantive” phone call with Vladimir Putin about efforts to end the war in Ukraine . Støre indicated afterwards that big differences remained. The two Nordic leaders said the call – a rare instance of direct contact between Putin and western leaders – was linked to upcoming talks between Russia , Ukraine and the US, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month. The ceasefire in Oleshky appears to be an attempt by the Kremlin to curry favour with Donald Trump ahead of the trilateral meeting and next week’s US midterm elections. The first lady, Melania Trump, requested the humanitarian mission, and in a post on X said it was brought forward by two days to allow the delivery of critical aid. Its geographical scope had been extended beyond Oleshky “within the Kherson region”, she added, to provide safe passage for convoys. Calls for a ceasefire were also issued by Pope Leo XIV, the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe . View image in fullscreen People board a bus in Kherson during a local ceasefire on Tuesday. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Between 1,500 and 2,000 people in the city have been living under a complete blockade by Russia. The last delivery of food to stores was in May, and many people are now starving and eating weeds. The Ukrainian military has airdropped food using drones. Locals say Russian security forces detain anyone who takes it. Russian soldiers have mined roads and use ruined buildings to coordinate round-the-clock strikes against Kherson. Some Oleshky residents have managed to escape, walking or cycling past bodies lying on the street and the burnt-out shells of numerous vehicles. Ukrainian observers say the Kremlin is planning a major propaganda tour this week in which Kyiv is blamed for Oleshky’s destruction. Trump-supporting US media channels have been invited to witness the evacuation, in which buses will take residents to occupied Crimea and Russia. Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled the city in 2022 and now, as a volunteer, helps others leave, said some residents have told her they fear Russian officials may “filter out” evacuees with pro-Ukraine views. “People say they are genuinely afraid that the Russians will check their phones and look for evidence of Ukrainian relatives or ties to the Armed Forces of Ukraine – something they have done repeatedly in other occupied territories,” Arkhipova told the Associated Press. The ceasefire does not extend to other parts of Ukraine. Overnight, Russia bombarded Kyiv with drones and ballistic missiles , killing at least one person and injuring 15. It hit a university campus, wounding students, as well as a bridge over the Dnipro and metro infrastructure. Ten other regions came under fire. View image in fullscreen A building damaged by an overnight Russian missile strike in Kyiv. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters The bridge remains closed to traffic, with some commuters walking across it to get to work. Writing on social media, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia “must stop dragging out this war” and said he welcomed European attempts to end it. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion He said Stubb and Støre had briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas clearly conveyed to the Russian leadership the need for genuine steps towards de-escalation, particularly when it comes to our energy sector and infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote. The Finnish-Norwegian initiative comes amid growing efforts by some European nations to establish a direct channel of communication with Moscow and secure a stronger European voice in negotiations. Stubb and Støre said they took part in the call as leaders of their respective countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole. European governments remain divided over whether direct engagement with Putin is worthwhile, at a time when Russia’s maximalist demands remain stubbornly unchanged. There is little agreement on who should lead such talks. Stubb is seen by some EU officials as a potential candidate. View image in fullscreen (L-r) Alexander Stubb, Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Jonas Gahr Støre in Oslo on 20 October. Photograph: Heiko Junge/EPA The divisions were laid bare shortly after news of the call emerged, when Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, criticised the move. “I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not agreed with any of us,” Frederiksen said. She added: “I see no signs that Russia wants peace with Europe – neither in the hybrid warfare it wages every day, nor in Ukraine, where brutal and aggressive strikes continue daily, claiming many lives.” Russia’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, said the Europeans had offered “nothing new”, and were simply trying to insert themselves in the negotiation process. Earlier this month Putin said he was willing to resume peace talks, but only on Russia’s hardline terms. They include the handover of the entire eastern Donbas region, including parts Russia has been unable to seize since 2014, as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces. Last week Zelenskyy said he was open to a peace agreement that would freeze the war along the current frontlines. “Yes, we are ready to stop this war as soon as possible,” he said in an interview with ABC News . He made clear that Ukraine would not recognise land seized and occupied by Russia as Russian. https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/10/1.text: Nuclear energy stocks are becoming closely tied to the data center build-out. Alphabet 's Google recently signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy , the U.S.'s largest nuclear operator, to support its growing power needs. After its Oct. 6 announcement, Constellation's stock soared 12%, and other nuclear energy stocks followed suit. One intriguing stock in the space is NuScale Power ( SMR -5.07% ) , an early-stage developer of small modular reactors (SMRs). As hyperscale data center operators search for dependable, carbon-free electricity, NuScale could offer investors another way to capitalize on the nuclear energy revival. The early-stage company trades below $6 per share and is largely story-driven, but one key catalyst could send the stock soaring. Image source: The Motley Fool. NuScale Power's stock has fallen drastically in 2026 NuScale's Power Modules are factory-built SMRs that are based on light-water reactor technology. Each module produces 77 MWe (megawatt-electric) of power and can be deployed in multiunit arrays to provide up to 924 MWe, enough to power 700,000 homes or heavy-duty infrastructure such as data centers or industrial plants. The stock surged last year as data center investments ramped up and the Department of Energy took steps to boost the nuclear energy industry. As part of these efforts, the U.S. has an aggressive goal of quadrupling nuclear energy capacity by 2050 and is building traditional power plants while accelerating the development of microreactor and SMR technology. After peaking at around $57 per share, NuScale is down over 90%. Several factors are driving the decline, including weakness in nuclear energy stocks, Fluor (an early investor in NuScale) exiting its stake , and a lack of further commitments for its technology. Here's one catalyst that could send NuScale soaring NuScale has one project in Romania , but it needs more in its pipeline to gain real traction. One deal that could send the stock soaring is with the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA). NuScale is working with ENTRA1 to develop power plants, and on Sept. 2, 2025, ENTRA1 signed a non-binding agreement with the TVA for up to 6 gigawatts (GW) of power across its service region. The 6 GW project would be the largest SMR deployment in the U.S. and would require deploying up to 72 NuScale Power Modules. A deal would transform NuScale's long-term outlook. CEO John Hopkins told investors during its Aug. 5 earnings call that the company is "extremely encouraged by our conversations that ENTRA1 and TVA are having" and that "TVA is actively engaged." NuScale hopes to secure firm commitments through power purchase agreements (PPAs), which could serve as a blueprint for future deals and get U.S. plant development underway. Until then, NuScale Power remains a risky, early-stage, story-driven stock , and its decline over the past year is a painful reminder. The stock is down 90% from its all-time high and could surge if it secures a much-coveted deal with TVA. But without a firm commitment, the stock may fall further, and investors should weigh its upside potential against the real risk of a further decline.
